response.title: what do i need to run my house on solar during an outage without a whole home system
response.answer:
You don't need a whole-home battery system like a Tesla Powerwall to run essential parts of your house on solar during a power outage.

There are several ways to do it, ranging from a portable solar generator that powers your refrigerator and Wi-Fi to a smaller backup system that powers selected household circuits.

The important distinction is that ordinary grid-tied solar panels automatically shut down during a power outage, even when the sun is shining. To use solar during an outage, you need equipment capable of operating independently of the grid.

1. Three ways to power your house during an outage
Shop

Option A — Portable power station

Simplest option

Approx. $1,000–$4,000+

A large rechargeable battery with a built-in inverter. Plug your refrigerator, router, lights, and other appliances directly into it. Add compatible solar panels to recharge during daylight.

Option B — Battery plus critical-loads panel

Approx. $3,000–$10,000+ installed

An electrician connects a battery inverter to selected circuits, such as your refrigerator, lights, internet, and garage door. You use normal wall switches and outlets during an outage.

Option C — Solar-only backup, without batteries

Cost depends on existing solar equipment

Certain specialized solar inverters can provide limited daytime power during an outage without batteries. This requires compatible hardware and grid-isolation equipment, and output varies with sunlight.

2. What equipment do you actually need?

For a small solar backup system that powers selected household circuits:

Conceptual layout for a solar-charged battery and selected household circuits. Actual connections and protection equipment depend on your inverter.

You generally need a solar array, a backup-capable inverter, a battery, a properly rated transfer or isolation device, and optionally a critical-loads subpanel.

For direct appliance connections to a portable power station, you can skip the transfer switch and subpanel. Never backfeed a house through a regular wall outlet.

3. How big a battery do you need?

Here's an example of running basic essentials for 24 hours.

2.9 kWh

A 4–5 kWh battery could cover roughly one day of these loads with some reserve, assuming no solar recharge. Actual runtime depends on appliance consumption, battery capacity, inverter losses, and starting surges.

You can adjust the daily load below:

Assumes 85% usable energy after losses and steady average consumption.
4. What if you already have rooftop solar?

This is where the choice of equipment becomes especially important.

If your panels are already installed, you may be able to add a compatible battery and backup controller to your existing system, without replacing the panels.

Alternatively, some systems, including compatible Enphase IQ8 microinverters, support daytime-only Sunlight Backup with additional control and isolation hardware.

The California Public Utilities Commission also notes that some existing solar installations can be retrofitted for outage operation. 
Web Training

5. Two questions that determine the best setup

Most of the house, including large appliances

These two details will determine whether you can get away with a simple portable battery or need a small permanently installed backup system.
